items.stem: A 31-year-old G3P1101 delivered spontaneously at 29 weeks in her last pregnancy after painless cervical dilation. At 21 weeks in this pregnancy, transvaginal ultrasonography shows a cervical length of 17 mm with no contractions or bleeding. Which management is recommended?
options: Ultrasound-indicated cerclage placement
Daily vaginal progesterone alone
Activity restriction with weekly cervical measurements
Nifedipine tocolysis until 34 weeks
items.explanation: A prior spontaneous preterm birth before 34 weeks combined with a cervical length under 25 mm before 24 weeks is the indication for an ultrasound-indicated cerclage, which lowers preterm birth. Progesterone alone is the choice when the cervix is short but there is no prior spontaneous preterm birth, activity restriction does not prevent early delivery, and maintenance tocolysis has no proven benefit in the absence of labor.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had three consecutive first-trimester losses. Which test is not recommended as part of the evaluation?
options: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies
Parental karyotype analysis
Three-dimensional pelvic ultrasonography
Factor V Leiden and protein S testing
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotypes when indicated, and imaging of the uterine cavity all identify causes that change management in recurrent pregnancy loss. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended because treating the abnormality has not been shown to improve live birth rates for early loss. Testing therefore adds cost and anxiety without changing management in this setting.

items.stem: A 9-month-old infant has profound hypotonia, a weak suck, and poor weight gain. Methylation testing of the 15q11-q13 region shows only the maternal pattern. Which condition is most likely?
options: Angelman syndrome
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
items.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternal 15q11-q13 contribution, by deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect, so only the maternal methylation pattern is seen. Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding give way to hyperphagia later. Angelman syndrome arises from loss of the maternal copy of the same region. Beckwith-Wiedemann involves imprinting at 11p15, and fragile X is a trinucleotide repeat disorder.

items.stem: A 50-year-old perimenopausal woman has had 4 months of difficulty falling asleep and early waking, with daytime fatigue. She has no depression, sleep apnea symptoms, or substance use. Which is the recommended first-line treatment?
options: Nightly zolpidem
Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
Diphenhydramine at bedtime
A nightly benzodiazepine
items.explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia and has durable benefit without drug risks, and it is combined with sleep hygiene and, when relevant, treatment of vasomotor symptoms. Sedative hypnotics such as zolpidem and benzodiazepines carry risks of dependence, falls, and next-day impairment and are reserved for short-term adjunctive use, and antihistamines lose effect quickly and cause anticholinergic effects.

items.stem: During suction dilation and curettage for an incomplete abortion, the cannula passes 4 cm beyond the sounded uterine depth and omental fat appears in the suction tubing. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
options: Observation with serial vital signs alone
Resume curettage with a sharp curette to finish evacuation
Discharge home with return precautions
Stop suction and perform laparoscopy to inspect the bowel and bladder
items.explanation: Fat or bowel in the suction tubing shows that suction was active when the uterus was perforated, so the bowel and mesentery may be injured. Laparoscopy, or laparotomy if the view is inadequate, is needed to inspect the bowel, bladder, and broad ligament. Observation is acceptable only when a blunt dilator or sound caused the perforation in a stable patient. Resuming curettage risks further injury, and discharge could miss an unrecognized bowel injury.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and a first-trimester hemoglobin A1c of 9.4% is counseled about fetal assessment. Which study is indicated?
options: Amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity
Fetal echocardiography at 18 to 22 weeks
Weekly umbilical artery Doppler from 20 weeks
Maternal serum bile acid testing
items.explanation: Pregestational diabetes with poor early glycemic control raises the risk of congenital heart disease, so a detailed fetal echocardiogram is offered in the second trimester. Fetal lung maturity testing is not used to evaluate anomalies. Umbilical artery Doppler is reserved for suspected growth restriction, and bile acid testing evaluates pruritus for cholestasis, a different problem than structural cardiac risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old nonsmoker has migraine with visual aura and wants a reliable contraceptive. Which method should be avoided?
options: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Etonogestrel implant
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Copper intrauterine device
items.explanation: Migraine with aura raises the baseline risk of ischemic stroke, and estrogen adds to it, so combined hormonal methods are in the highest category of the medical eligibility criteria and should not be used. Progestin-only methods, including the levonorgestrel device and the implant, are acceptable. The copper device is nonhormonal and also acceptable, so the choice can follow her preference for bleeding pattern.

items.stem: A healthy 29-year-old at 30 weeks of gestation has routine laboratory testing. Which result is expected as a normal finding of pregnancy rather than a sign of disease?
options: Serum creatinine of 0.5 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen of 24 mg/dL
Fibrinogen of 180 mg/dL
Platelet count of 80,000 per microliter
items.explanation: Glomerular filtration rises by 40 to 50 percent in pregnancy, so creatinine and urea nitrogen fall, and a creatinine near 0.5 mg/dL is normal while 0.9 or more suggests renal disease. Fibrinogen climbs to 400 to 600 mg/dL, so a value of 180 is abnormal and suggests abruption or coagulopathy. A urea nitrogen of 24 exceeds the usual pregnancy range, and platelets below 100,000 warrant evaluation.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman at average risk for colorectal cancer asks when to begin screening. Which recommendation is appropriate?
options: Begin at age 50
Screen only if rectal bleeding develops
Annual serum CA 19-9 measurement
Begin now, with colonoscopy every 10 years or an alternative stool-based test
items.explanation: Current guidance recommends beginning colorectal cancer screening at age 45 for average-risk adults, using colonoscopy every 10 years or a stool-based test at the appropriate interval. Waiting until age 50 is outdated, and symptom-triggered testing is diagnostic rather than screening. CA 19-9 is not a validated screening marker. Screening continues at intervals after a normal result.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is placed in steep Trendelenburg position under general anesthesia for robotic hysterectomy with carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum. Which physiologic change is expected?
options: Increased functional residual capacity with falling end-tidal carbon dioxide
Reduced intraocular pressure
Reduced functional residual capacity with rising end-tidal carbon dioxide
Decreased systemic vascular resistance with falling blood pressure
items.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning push the diaphragm upward, decrease functional residual capacity and compliance, and carbon dioxide absorption raises end-tidal carbon dioxide, so ventilation is adjusted. Intraocular and intracranial pressures rise rather than fall, and systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure typically increase from insufflation and catecholamine release, so the opposite changes would not be expected.

items.stem: A 28-year-old healthy woman at 34 weeks in October asks how to protect her newborn from respiratory syncytial virus. Which option is appropriate?
options: A single dose of maternal RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks during the seasonal window
Maternal RSV vaccine at 12 weeks
A live attenuated vaccine given to the newborn
No protective option exists before 6 months of age
items.explanation: A single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine given at 32 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks, in the seasonal window from September through January, passes antibodies to the infant and lowers severe lower respiratory disease in early months. Earlier vaccination is not the approved window. A live newborn vaccine does not exist, and infant monoclonal antibody is the alternative, so some option does exist.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has hirsutism, acne, and irregular menses since menarche. Total testosterone is mildly raised, DHEA sulfate is normal, and prolactin and thyrotropin are normal. Which additional test is needed to exclude a mimic of polycystic ovary syndrome?
options: Adrenal computed tomography
A follicular phase morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone level
An overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Serum estradiol on cycle day 3
items.explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency mimics it with hirsutism and irregular cycles. A follicular phase morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone screens for it, and a markedly elevated value confirms the diagnosis. Adrenal imaging is reserved for a markedly raised DHEA sulfate or rapid virilization, dexamethasone suppression addresses Cushing syndrome, and estradiol does not discriminate.

items.stem: In a case-control study, 40 of 100 cases and 20 of 100 controls were exposed to a drug. What is the approximate odds ratio of exposure?
items.explanation: The odds ratio equals the odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds in controls. Cases have 40 exposed and 60 unexposed, giving 0.67, and controls have 20 exposed and 80 unexposed, giving 0.25, so the ratio is about 2.7. The value 2.0 is the simple ratio of proportions, 1.5 inverts the case odds, and 0.37 is the reciprocal.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman reports that her mother had ovarian cancer at 50 and her sister had breast cancer at 38. She has no symptoms. What is the best next step?
options: Annual CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasonography screening
Refer for genetic counseling and germline testing
Bilateral prophylactic mastectomy now
Reassurance and routine screening only
items.explanation: A family history of early-onset breast cancer and ovarian cancer meets criteria for hereditary risk assessment, and counseling with germline testing guides screening and risk-reducing options. CA-125 with ultrasonography does not reduce ovarian cancer mortality. Surgery is premature without a known variant, and routine screening alone underestimates her risk and misses the chance for tailored care.

items.stem: Three weeks after cesarean birth through a Pfannenstiel incision, a woman has sharp burning pain near the lateral end of the scar that radiates to the groin and labia, worsens with standing, and eases with hip flexion. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Femoral nerve injury
Obturator nerve injury
Ilioinguinal or iliohypogastric nerve entrapment
Incisional hernia
items.explanation: Burning pain at the lateral incision with radiation to the groin and labia that eases with hip flexion typifies entrapment of the ilioinguinal or iliohypogastric nerve in scar or suture after a low transverse incision. Femoral and obturator injuries cause motor and sensory deficits in the thigh, not pain at the scar. An incisional hernia produces a bulge rather than a neuropathic distribution.

items.stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 36 0/7 weeks has a normal growth scan, a reactive nonstress test, intact membranes, and a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm. There is no other complication. What is the best plan?
options: Delivery between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks
Expectant management with weekly pocket measurement until 40 weeks
Oral hydration and repeat imaging, then delivery at 41 weeks
Amnioinfusion now and delivery at 39 weeks
items.explanation: Isolated oligohydramnios with otherwise normal findings is an indication for delivery between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks because of the risk of cord compression and stillbirth. Hydration may transiently raise fluid but does not justify prolonging the pregnancy. Amnioinfusion is a labor intervention for variable decelerations, not an antepartum treatment, and waiting for 40 weeks accepts avoidable risk.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 5 months of amenorrhea and hot flushes. Follicle-stimulating hormone is 68 mIU/mL and 55 mIU/mL one month apart, and prolactin and thyrotropin are normal. Karyotype and FMR1 testing are sent. What is the best long-term management?
options: No hormone therapy because of breast cancer risk
Low-dose estrogen for five years only
Estrogen and progestogen therapy until about age 51
Clomiphene citrate to induce ovulation for pregnancy
items.explanation: This is primary ovarian insufficiency. Without estrogen, the risk of osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline rises, so hormone therapy is advised until the average age of natural menopause. The breast cancer risk that applies to older women does not apply to replacement at this age. A fixed five-year course ends early, and clomiphene cannot stimulate follicles that are depleted.

items.stem: A 33-year-old multipara has a postpartum hemorrhage after vaginal birth and receives uterotonics and an intrauterine balloon. A hospital quality committee reviews her chart. Which feature meets the standard screening criterion for severe maternal morbidity?
options: Transfusion of four or more units of red cells
Estimated blood loss of 1,000 mL
Placement of an intrauterine balloon
A hemoglobin of 9 g/dL on the first postpartum day
items.explanation: National screening criteria for severe maternal morbidity flag transfusion of four or more units of blood products and admission to intensive care, among others, so cases can be reviewed for system lessons. Blood loss of 1,000 mL defines hemorrhage but is not itself a screening criterion. Balloon tamponade and a modest postpartum hemoglobin are expected parts of care and do not trigger review by themselves.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman who had chickenpox in childhood and has never received a zoster vaccine asks about preventing shingles. She is immunocompetent. Which recommendation is correct?
options: Live zoster vaccine as a single dose
Recombinant zoster vaccine, two doses 2 to 6 months apart
No vaccine until age 65
Varicella zoster immune globulin now
items.explanation: The recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended as a two-dose series, 2 to 6 months apart, for adults aged 50 and older, whether or not they recall chickenpox, and it is not a live vaccine. The live zoster vaccine is no longer used in the United States, waiting until 65 leaves the earlier high-risk years unprotected, and immune globulin is for postexposure prevention of varicella in susceptible people, not for shingles prevention.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 had an elective McDonald cerclage placed at 14 weeks because of a prior painless second-trimester loss. She is now at 35 weeks with intact membranes, no contractions, and an uncomplicated course. What is the plan for the cerclage?
options: Remove it today because the fetus is now viable
Leave it in place until labor begins
Leave it until 41 weeks and remove it before induction
Remove it electively at 36 to 37 weeks
items.explanation: An elective McDonald cerclage is removed at 36 to 37 weeks, when the pregnancy is near term and the stitch is no longer needed, so that spontaneous labor does not cause cervical laceration or uterine rupture. Removing it earlier in an uncomplicated pregnancy forfeits its benefit, and leaving it until labor or beyond term risks cervical tearing and delays recognition of labor. Earlier removal is reserved for rupture of membranes, infection, or labor.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a high-risk cell-free DNA result and asks a colleague to perform chorionic villus sampling at 8 weeks. What is the main reason to wait until at least 10 weeks?
options: Villi do not contain fetal cells before 10 weeks
Maternal cell contamination makes the karyotype unreliable
Earlier sampling is associated with limb reduction defects
The risk of Rh alloimmunization is higher before 10 weeks
items.explanation: Chorionic villus sampling is performed from 10 0/7 to 13 6/7 weeks. Procedures before 10 weeks have been associated with transverse limb reduction defects, so the test is delayed. Villi contain fetal-origin cells from early in pregnancy, and contamination is a general technical risk rather than a reason tied to this window. Rh immune globulin is given when indicated regardless of the procedure timing.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has had heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche, frequent nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL with a normal platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time. Which test is most appropriate next?
options: Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity testing
Transvaginal ultrasonography for fibroids
Endometrial biopsy to exclude hyperplasia
Serum testosterone and DHEA sulfate with 17-hydroxyprogesterone
items.explanation: Heavy bleeding from menarche with mucosal bleeding suggests an inherited bleeding disorder, and von Willebrand disease is the most common. Normal platelet count and screening clotting times do not exclude it, so specific factor testing is needed. Fibroids and endometrial hyperplasia are unlikely in an adolescent, and androgen testing evaluates hirsutism, not a bleeding disorder.

items.stem: During an oophorectomy for a large left ovarian mass, the surgeon ligates the ovarian vessels at the infundibulopelvic ligament. Into which vessel does the left ovarian vein drain?
options: The inferior vena cava directly
The left internal iliac vein
The left common iliac vein
The left renal vein
items.explanation: The right ovarian vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, whereas the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein, an asymmetry that follows the embryologic course of the gonadal veins. The ovarian arteries arise from the aorta just below the renal arteries, and the internal iliac system supplies the uterus through the uterine artery. This pathway matters when ligating the pedicle and when interpreting left-sided venous thrombosis.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with no known risk factors asks whether she should be screened for hepatitis C. She is not pregnant and has never been tested. What is the recommendation?
options: Screening only if her transaminases are elevated
A one-time hepatitis C antibody test with reflex confirmatory testing
Annual screening for all adults
No screening until age 50
items.explanation: Hepatitis C screening is recommended once for all adults, with reflex nucleic acid testing when the antibody is positive, and again in each pregnancy, with repeat testing when risk continues. Restricting testing to risk groups or abnormal liver tests misses many infections, annual testing is for ongoing risk such as injection drug use, and the infection is curable with direct-acting antivirals, so detection changes the outcome.

items.stem: Before abdominal hysterectomy, which approach to hair removal and skin antisepsis best reduces surgical site infection?
options: Shave with a razor the night before and use povidone-iodine alone
Apply a depilatory cream the week before surgery
Soak the abdomen in soap and water the night before
Clip hair only if needed, just before surgery, and use a chlorhexidine-based skin preparation
items.explanation: Hair is removed only when it interferes with the incision, and then by clipping immediately before surgery, since razor shaving creates microabrasions that harbor bacteria. A chlorhexidine-based skin preparation is superior to povidone-iodine for preventing infection. Depilatory creams can cause skin reactions, and soaking with soap and water does not provide effective antisepsis or lasting skin cleansing.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 37 weeks with severe hypertension has a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure in triage, now ended. After airway support, which medication is first line?
options: Phenytoin intravenous loading dose
Diazepam as the first-line anticonvulsant
Magnesium sulfate, 4 to 6 g intravenous loading dose
Oral nifedipine alone
items.explanation: Eclampsia is treated with magnesium sulfate, which reduces recurrent seizures more effectively than phenytoin or benzodiazepines and is started with a 4 to 6 g loading dose followed by an infusion. Benzodiazepines are reserved for a seizure that persists despite magnesium. Antihypertensives treat pressure but do not prevent further seizures. Magnesium also continues for 24 hours after delivery to prevent recurrence.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a stable unruptured ectopic pregnancy receives single-dose methotrexate. The hCG is 2,400 on day 1, 2,600 on day 4, and 2,350 on day 7. What is the next step?
options: Give a second methotrexate dose
Continue weekly hCG without further treatment
Perform dilation and curettage
Begin vaginal misoprostol
items.explanation: With the single-dose protocol, hCG is measured on days 4 and 7, and a decline of at least 15% between those days predicts success. Here the fall is under 10%, so a second dose is given. A transient early rise is common and expected. Observation alone would accept probable treatment failure, curettage does not remove a tubal pregnancy, and misoprostol is not an ectopic treatment.

items.stem: A small trial finds no significant difference in cesarean rates between two induction methods (p = 0.20), although the observed difference is clinically meaningful. Which error is most likely?
options: Type I error, because the p value exceeds 0.05
Type II error, because the study may be underpowered
Selection bias in the control arm
Lead-time bias
items.explanation: A nonsignificant result in a small trial with a meaningful observed difference raises the possibility of a type II error, failing to detect a true effect because power was insufficient. A type I error means falsely declaring a difference, which did not happen here. Selection bias and lead-time bias are unrelated to sample size and to this result.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with no diabetes or cardiovascular disease has an LDL cholesterol of 195 mg/dL on two fasting measurements. Her father had a myocardial infarction at age 48. Blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. What is the best treatment?
options: Lifestyle changes alone for 12 months
Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention
Niacin as monotherapy
High-intensity statin therapy
items.explanation: An LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL or higher suggests familial hypercholesterolemia, and statin therapy is indicated regardless of calculated 10-year risk, using a high-intensity statin to lower LDL by at least 50 percent. Lifestyle changes alone cannot achieve that reduction, aspirin is not recommended for primary prevention in this setting, and niacin has not improved outcomes when used instead of a statin.

items.stem: Four days after a laparoscopic hysterectomy using monopolar electrosurgery, a 44-year-old woman has a temperature of 38.8 C, worsening abdominal pain, and a rigid abdomen. The white blood cell count is 19,000 per microliter. What is the most likely cause and evaluation?
options: Atelectasis managed with incentive spirometry
Thermal bowel injury needing imaging and exploration
Urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics
Ileus managed with bowel rest alone
items.explanation: Thermal injury to bowel is often outside the surgeon's view and declares itself three to seven days after surgery as fever, worsening pain, leukocytosis, and peritonitis. A rigid abdomen is not explained by ileus or atelectasis, and it calls for computed tomography and usually exploration with repair or resection. Atelectasis and urinary infection do not cause peritonitis, and managing a perforation with bowel rest alone allows sepsis to progress.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with diet-controlled gestational diabetes delivered 2 days ago, and her glucose values are now normal. When should she be tested for persistent diabetes?
options: A hemoglobin A1c before hospital discharge today
No testing, because gestational diabetes resolves after birth
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 4 to 12 weeks after delivery
A fasting glucose only after one year
items.explanation: Gestational diabetes marks a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, so a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is advised 4 to 12 weeks after delivery, and normal results still need repeat testing every 1 to 3 years. A hemoglobin A1c at discharge is unreliable after blood loss and too early. Assuming resolution without testing misses persistent disease, and waiting a year delays diagnosis.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a temperature of 38.9 C, pelvic pain, and a 6 cm complex adnexal mass consistent with a tubo-ovarian abscess. She is hemodynamically stable with no signs of rupture and is not pregnant. What is the best initial management?
options: Hospital admission with intravenous antibiotics
Immediate laparotomy with hysterectomy
Outpatient oral doxycycline and metronidazole
Percutaneous drainage without antibiotics
items.explanation: A stable patient with an unruptured tubo-ovarian abscess is admitted for broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics with anaerobic coverage, such as cefoxitin or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole, and image-guided drainage is added if she does not improve within 48 to 72 hours. Surgery is reserved for rupture or failed drainage, outpatient therapy is inadequate for an abscess this size, and drainage without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated.

items.stem: A resident notices on a routine postoperative abdominal radiograph that a surgical sponge was left in a patient after hysterectomy. The attending suggests waiting until the patient is discharged before mentioning it. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait for symptoms before telling the patient
Disclose promptly to the patient and report the event
Disclose only if she develops complications
Record the finding in the chart without informing her
items.explanation: A retained surgical item is a reportable adverse event, and prompt, honest disclosure to the patient is an ethical duty that preserves trust and allows timely removal. The event is entered in the institutional safety reporting system for root cause analysis, with an apology and a plan for correction. Delaying disclosure, telling her only if harm occurs, or charting without informing her is nondisclosure and violates professional standards.

items.stem: A 19-year-old college student has had amenorrhea for 8 months. Her body mass index is 16 kg/m2, heart rate is 48 beats per minute, and she restricts food intake while exercising daily. Pregnancy test is negative and bone density shows a Z-score of minus 2.2. Which intervention is most important for her bone health?
options: A combined oral contraceptive to restore bone density
Bisphosphonate therapy
High-dose calcium supplementation alone
Nutritional rehabilitation with weight restoration
items.explanation: Amenorrhea from anorexia nervosa reflects estrogen deficiency from energy deficit and causes low bone density, and the treatment is weight restoration through nutritional rehabilitation with mental health care, the only intervention shown to restore menses and recover bone. Combined pills do not improve bone density in this setting and can mask the amenorrhea, bisphosphonates are avoided in women who may become pregnant, and calcium alone cannot compensate for energy deficiency.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with hypertension controlled on a thiazide and no other medical problems is scheduled for elective abdominal hysterectomy. She climbs two flights of stairs without symptoms and has a Revised Cardiac Risk Index of 0. What is the appropriate preoperative cardiac evaluation?
options: Exercise stress echocardiography
Coronary angiography
Proceed without additional cardiac testing
Starting a beta blocker on the morning of surgery
items.explanation: A functional capacity of about four metabolic equivalents, such as climbing two flights of stairs, together with a Revised Cardiac Risk Index of 0, predicts low risk, so she can proceed without stress testing or angiography. Testing is reserved for patients in whom the result would change management, and a beta blocker is continued if already taken but is not started on the day of surgery.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman 3 months after delivery has palpitations, tremor, and weight loss. Thyrotropin is suppressed, free thyroxine is elevated, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is negative, and radioactive iodine uptake is low. The thyroid is painless and not enlarged. What is the best management?
options: A beta blocker for symptoms and repeat thyroid tests in 4 to 8 weeks
Methimazole for 12 months
Radioactive iodine ablation
Total thyroidectomy
items.explanation: Painless thyrotoxicosis within a year of delivery with negative receptor antibodies and low iodine uptake is postpartum thyroiditis, a destructive process in which stored hormone leaks from the gland. The thyrotoxic phase is self-limited, so symptoms are controlled with a beta blocker and thyroid function is rechecked, because a hypothyroid phase often follows. Antithyroid drugs and ablation treat overproduction, which is absent, and surgery is unnecessary.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has progressively severe cyclic pelvic pain despite regular menses. MRI shows a unicornuate uterus with a noncommunicating rudimentary horn containing endometrium. What is the best treatment?
options: Hysteroscopic septum resection
Long-term suppression with a GnRH agonist alone
Vaginal dilators
Laparoscopic excision of the rudimentary horn
items.explanation: A noncommunicating rudimentary horn with functional endometrium traps menstrual blood, causing hematometra, endometriosis, and a risk of ectopic pregnancy, so it is excised laparoscopically, usually with its ipsilateral tube. Septum resection treats a different anomaly. Hormonal suppression only postpones the problem, and vaginal dilators are for vaginal agenesis. Early surgery relieves pain and protects fertility by preventing pelvic disease.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with endometriosis receives monthly injections of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist and develops hot flushes. Which mechanism explains the suppression of ovarian estradiol production?
options: Direct blockade of the ovarian estrogen receptor
Receptor desensitization after an initial flare
Inhibition of aromatase in granulosa cells
Increased hepatic clearance of circulating estradiol
items.explanation: GnRH normally acts in pulses, and continuous exposure from a long-acting agonist first causes a transient rise in LH and FSH, then downregulates pituitary receptors, so gonadotropins and estradiol fall to menopausal levels. The agonist does not block estrogen receptors, aromatase inhibition is a property of letrozole, and the hormonal fall is central rather than due to faster hepatic clearance.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman who lives alone reports one fall in the past year without injury. She walks slowly, has osteopenia, and has no dementia. Which intervention most effectively reduces her risk of future falls?
options: Daily calcium supplementation alone
A bedtime sedative to improve sleep
A supervised exercise program emphasizing balance and strength
Annual repeat bone density testing
items.explanation: Exercise programs that train balance, gait, and strength have the strongest evidence for preventing falls in older adults, and they are combined with medication review, vision assessment, and home safety changes. Calcium alone does not prevent falls, sedatives raise fall risk, and repeating bone density testing measures fracture risk without changing the likelihood of falling.

items.stem: At the end of an abdominal hysterectomy for a large fibroid uterus, cystoscopy after intravenous dye shows no efflux from the left ureteral orifice after 15 minutes, while the right side is normal. What is the best next step?
options: Retrograde catheterization of the ureter to locate the obstruction
Close the abdomen and recheck urine output the next morning
Give furosemide and repeat cystoscopy in a week
Place a suprapubic catheter and observe for 48 hours
items.explanation: Absent efflux suggests ureteral ligation, kinking, or transection, and recognizing it at surgery avoids later hydronephrosis, fistula, or loss of the kidney. Passing a catheter retrograde finds the level of obstruction, and the suture is released or the ureter repaired or reimplanted with urology help. Waiting, diuresis, or bladder drainage cannot relieve a blocked ureter.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has persistent lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies, three early pregnancy losses, and no history of thrombosis. She is now 7 weeks pregnant. Which regimen is recommended?
options: Low-dose aspirin alone throughout pregnancy
Therapeutic warfarin from the first trimester onward
Prednisone with hydroxychloroquine alone
Prophylactic anticoagulation plus low-dose aspirin
items.explanation: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome without thrombosis is treated with prophylactic-dose anticoagulation and low-dose aspirin, which improves live birth rates. Aspirin alone is less effective than the combination. Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy, and it is not used for this indication. Corticosteroids do not improve outcomes and add maternal and fetal risk, while hydroxychloroquine is an adjunct rather than a substitute.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a cotest with negative cytology and a positive HPV test, with genotyping showing HPV 16. What is the next step?
options: Repeat cotesting in 1 year
Repeat cotesting in 3 years
Colposcopy
Loop electrosurgical excision
items.explanation: A positive HPV 16 result carries a high immediate risk of precancer even with normal cytology, so colposcopy is recommended without waiting. Repeat testing in one year is the plan for other HPV types with negative cytology. A three-year return applies to negative results. Excision is not performed without histologic confirmation of high-grade disease in most circumstances.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman was treated for uncomplicated chlamydial cervicitis with doxycycline, and her partner was treated. She is asymptomatic. When should she be retested?
options: One week after finishing therapy to confirm cure
About 3 months after treatment
Only after 12 months, with her next routine screening
Never, since the partner was treated
items.explanation: Women treated for chlamydia have high rates of reinfection, so retesting about 3 months after treatment is recommended regardless of partner treatment. A test of cure within weeks is not advised for nonpregnant patients because residual nucleic acid causes false positives. Waiting a year allows undetected reinfection to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, and treating the partner does not remove the need to retest.

items.stem: After a 5-hour robotic hysterectomy in steep Trendelenburg position with shoulder braces and both arms abducted at 100 degrees, a 52-year-old woman has weakness of the hand and numbness along the medial forearm. Which structure was most likely injured?
options: Brachial plexus
Femoral nerve
Obturator nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
items.explanation: Steep Trendelenburg position with shoulder braces and arms abducted beyond 90 degrees stretches and compresses the brachial plexus, producing upper limb weakness and sensory loss. The femoral, obturator, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves are lower extremity nerves injured by hip flexion, retractors, or lithotomy positioning, and none causes hand symptoms. Prevention relies on padding, neutral alignment, and avoiding shoulder braces and extreme arm abduction.

items.stem: A 28-year-old kindergarten teacher at 20 weeks learns that several pupils have erythema infectiosum. She has no symptoms. Serology shows parvovirus B19 IgG positive and IgM negative. What is the most appropriate counseling?
options: Weekly middle cerebral artery Doppler studies until delivery
Intravenous immune globulin to prevent fetal anemia
She is immune, so no fetal surveillance is needed
Termination should be discussed because infection is likely
items.explanation: A positive IgG with a negative IgM indicates past infection and lasting immunity, and about half of adult women are already immune, so the fetus is not at risk and no intervention is needed. Doppler surveillance is reserved for documented acute infection, because parvovirus can cause fetal anemia and hydrops. Immune globulin has no proven role, and immune serology never indicates termination.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has intense vulvar itching. Biopsy confirms lichen sclerosus. Examination shows pale, thin, crinkled skin and fusion of the labia minora. Which treatment is first-line?
options: Low-potency topical hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid ointment
Topical estradiol cream
Oral fluconazole
items.explanation: Lichen sclerosus is treated with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol, tapered to maintenance, which relieves itching and halts scarring. Low-potency steroids are inadequate. Estrogen helps atrophy but does not treat the disease, and fluconazole addresses candida, not an inflammatory dermatosis. Long-term follow up is needed because squamous cell carcinoma can arise in affected skin.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who is not pregnant uses heroin daily and asks for help to stop. She has no other medical problems. Which treatment is most effective at reducing mortality?
options: Buprenorphine or methadone maintenance with counseling
Detoxification alone followed by discharge
A short course of clonidine alone
Counseling without any medication
items.explanation: Medication for opioid use disorder with buprenorphine or methadone reduces mortality, relapse, and infectious complications and is continued rather than tapered quickly, with naloxone supplied for overdose rescue and counseling offered alongside. Detoxification alone has high relapse and overdose rates after tolerance falls, clonidine only blunts withdrawal symptoms, and counseling alone omits the treatment with the best evidence.

items.stem: During laparoscopic hysterectomy, placement of a lateral 5 mm trocar causes brisk bleeding along the abdominal wall with an expanding hematoma, from the inferior epigastric artery. What is the best management?
options: Remove the trocar and observe without intervention
Apply pressure with gauze and close the skin
Convert to a different surgical procedure
Full-thickness suture around the site or transfascial balloon tamponade
items.explanation: Inferior epigastric injury from a lateral port is controlled by direct measures, either a full-thickness figure-of-eight suture around the port site or tamponade with a transfascial balloon catheter, with ligation of the vessel if needed. Observation risks a large rectus sheath hematoma, and skin pressure does not control a deep arterial bleed. Changing the planned operation does not stop the bleeding.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with HIV taking antiretroviral therapy has a viral load below 50 copies per milliliter at 36 weeks. Which statement about delivery is correct?
options: Vaginal delivery is appropriate and intrapartum zidovudine is not required
Scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks is mandatory
Intravenous zidovudine is required for every woman with HIV
Delivery should be induced at 34 weeks
items.explanation: With a suppressed viral load, the risk of perinatal transmission is under 1 percent, so delivery follows obstetric indications and intrapartum zidovudine is not needed when the load is below 1,000 copies. Cesarean for HIV is advised for loads above 1,000 near delivery. Intravenous zidovudine is not universal, and preterm induction adds neonatal risk with no benefit.

items.stem: A 41-year-old BRCA1 carrier has had risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy and has severe vasomotor symptoms. She has never had breast cancer. Which statement about treatment is correct?
options: Estrogen is contraindicated permanently
Only testosterone therapy is acceptable
Symptoms must be left untreated for 10 years
Systemic estrogen therapy is acceptable until the usual age of natural menopause
items.explanation: In BRCA carriers without breast cancer, surgical menopause causes severe symptoms and long-term health risks, and systemic estrogen is acceptable until about the average age of natural menopause, with no evident rise in breast cancer risk. Permanent contraindication, testosterone alone, or years of untreated symptoms are unsupported and harm bone, cardiovascular, and quality-of-life outcomes. Continued therapy is reassessed periodically and is not given for life.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and prediabetes plans to try to conceive in 6 months and asks about semaglutide for weight loss. Which counseling is correct?
options: It is safe to continue throughout pregnancy
Use contraception while taking it and stop it at least 2 months before trying to conceive
It is the preferred drug for limiting gestational weight gain
Early pregnancy exposure requires no change in plans
items.explanation: Semaglutide is not recommended in pregnancy because of limited safety data and animal findings, and its long half-life means it should be stopped at least 2 months before a planned conception, with effective contraception in the meantime. It is not a treatment for gestational weight gain. Continuing it or ignoring early exposure disregards the recommended washout.

items.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and malaise followed by jaundice. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Glucose is 48 mg/dL, bilirubin is 5.2 mg/dL, prothrombin time is prolonged, and ammonia is elevated. Platelets are 140,000 per microliter. What is the best management?
options: Ursodeoxycholic acid with delivery at 39 weeks
Magnesium sulfate with expectant care until term
Stabilize with glucose and blood products, then deliver promptly
Cholecystectomy during the third trimester
items.explanation: Third-trimester nausea, jaundice, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and hyperammonemia without hypertension characterize acute fatty liver of pregnancy, a life-threatening disorder managed with supportive care, correction of glucose and clotting factors, and prompt delivery of the baby once she is stable. Ursodeoxycholic acid treats cholestasis, which does not cause hypoglycemia or coagulopathy, magnesium sulfate treats preeclampsia, and delaying delivery allows liver failure to progress.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman finds a firm, mobile 2-cm breast mass. She has no family history of breast cancer. Which is the best first imaging study?
options: Diagnostic breast ultrasonography
Screening mammography
Breast magnetic resonance imaging
Diagnostic mammography with tomosynthesis
items.explanation: In women younger than 30 with a palpable mass, ultrasonography is the first study because dense breast tissue limits mammography and it distinguishes solid from cystic lesions without radiation. Screening mammography is not designed to evaluate a symptomatic mass. Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for problem solving or high-risk screening, and diagnostic mammography is added for women aged 30 and older.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has an LDL cholesterol of 118 mg/dL and no history of cardiovascular disease. She is a nonsmoker with blood pressure of 124/78 mm Hg. Which therapy is most appropriate?
options: Lifestyle changes only until LDL reaches 190 mg/dL
Ezetimibe as monotherapy
Aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention
Moderate-intensity statin therapy
items.explanation: Adults aged 40 to 75 with diabetes should receive at least a moderate-intensity statin regardless of baseline LDL, and higher intensity is used with added risk factors. Waiting for LDL of 190 applies to a different primary prevention group. Ezetimibe alone lacks outcome data as monotherapy, and routine aspirin for primary prevention carries bleeding risk that outweighs benefit for most.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 37 0/7 weeks has a frank breech presentation confirmed by ultrasonography. Amniotic fluid volume is normal, the placenta is posterior, and the tracing is reassuring. She has no contraindication to labor. What should be offered?
options: Scheduled cesarean birth now, without any attempt at version
Moxibustion as the primary method of turning the fetus
External cephalic version
Induction of labor to deliver the breech fetus now
items.explanation: External cephalic version is offered at or after 36 0/7 weeks to women with a breech fetus and no contraindication, and it succeeds in about half of attempts, lowering the cesarean rate. Contraindications include placenta previa, ruptured membranes, and nonreassuring testing, none of which applies. Cesarean birth before 39 weeks and induction to deliver a breech fetus are not appropriate, and moxibustion has not been shown to be reliable.

items.stem: On pelvic organ prolapse quantification, a woman with a total vaginal length of 9 cm has a leading edge of prolapse that reaches 3 cm beyond the hymen at maximal strain. What is the stage?
options: Stage 0 or I
Stage III
Stage II
Stage IV
items.explanation: Stage III is defined by a leading edge more than 1 cm beyond the hymen but not protruding farther than 2 cm less than the total vaginal length. Here the leading edge is at plus 3, which lies beyond plus 1 and short of plus 7, so the stage is III. Stage II places the leading edge within 1 cm of the hymen, and stage IV is complete eversion.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with no chronic disease has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B and has no history of infection. She asks whether vaccination is advisable. What is the recommendation?
options: Complete a hepatitis B vaccine series
Vaccinate only if she is a health care worker
A single injection of immune globulin instead
No vaccine, because routine vaccination ends at age 40
items.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended routinely for all unvaccinated adults through age 59 regardless of risk factors, and for older adults with risk factors or on request. A risk assessment is not required before vaccination, immune globulin is passive postexposure protection and not a substitute for the series, and routine vaccination does not stop at age 40.

items.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks in early labor has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds. Afterward, blood pressure is 172/112 mm Hg and the fetal heart rate shows a transient bradycardia that recovers. Which is the most appropriate first-line seizure treatment?
options: Intravenous phenytoin
Intravenous diazepam as the sole agent
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Intravenous labetalol alone
items.explanation: A seizure in a woman with new severe hypertension is eclampsia until proved otherwise, and magnesium sulfate is both the treatment and the prophylaxis, being more effective than phenytoin or diazepam in preventing recurrence. Blood pressure is lowered afterward with labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine, and delivery is planned once she is stable. The transient bradycardia usually recovers, so emergency cesarean birth is not the first step.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a routine urine culture growing Escherichia coli at 100,000 colony-forming units per milliliter. She has no urinary symptoms, is not pregnant, and is not scheduled for a urologic procedure. What is the appropriate management?
options: Oral nitrofurantoin for 5 days
A single dose of fosfomycin
Intravenous ceftriaxone for 7 days
No antibiotic treatment
items.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in nonpregnant women should not be screened for or treated, because treatment does not reduce symptomatic infection and promotes resistance and adverse effects. Exceptions are pregnancy and before invasive urologic procedures with mucosal trauma. Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, and ceftriaxone all expose her to risk without any benefit. Treating a positive culture without symptoms is therefore a common source of overtreatment.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman is accompanied to clinic by an older man who answers every question for her and will not leave the room. She has no identification, appears frightened, and has had three sexually transmitted infections in 6 months. What is the best approach?
options: Ask the man to confirm her history and proceed
Interview her alone and offer a hotline
Confront the man about trafficking in front of her
Report to the police without speaking to her
items.explanation: Controlled movement, no identification, a companion who speaks for her, and repeated infections are red flags for human trafficking. The clinician should find a way to interview her alone, use a trauma-informed approach, offer a hotline and referral resources, and follow reporting rules, because confronting the companion can endanger her. Relying on his history ignores the warning signs, and bypassing her removes her agency and may prompt retaliation.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 at 37 weeks asks about vaginal birth. She has had two cesarean births, the first through a classical uterine incision and the second through a low transverse incision. What is the best counseling?
options: Scheduled repeat cesarean birth
Trial of labor with continuous fetal monitoring
Cervical ripening with misoprostol followed by induction
Trial of labor with early epidural analgesia
items.explanation: A prior classical or T-shaped uterine incision carries a markedly higher risk of rupture in labor, so these patients are delivered by planned repeat cesarean, usually at 36 to 37 weeks. Two low transverse cesareans alone would not preclude a trial of labor, but the classical scar does, and monitoring or epidural placement does not remove the risk. Misoprostol is avoided after any uterine surgery because it raises the rupture risk further.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl with Tanner stage 4 breasts and no menses has had cyclic lower abdominal pain for 4 months. A bluish bulging membrane is seen at the introitus. What is the treatment?
options: Combined oral contraceptive to suppress menses
Serial vaginal dilator therapy
Hymenotomy with drainage of the retained blood
Vaginoplasty with a skin graft
items.explanation: An imperforate hymen is the most common obstructive anomaly and presents at puberty with cyclic pain and hematocolpos behind a bulging membrane. Surgical incision of the hymen drains the blood and restores outflow. Suppressing menses leaves the obstruction, and dilators or skin-graft vaginoplasty are for vaginal agenesis, which has a normal-appearing introitus with no bulge.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 38 0/7 weeks has an uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. The first twin is cephalic and the second is breech, with similar estimated weights of 2,900 g and 3,100 g. What is the best delivery plan?
options: Cesarean birth is required because the second twin is breech
Offer a trial of vaginal birth with a plan for the second twin
Cesarean birth is required for every twin pregnancy
Delay delivery until 41 weeks to allow the second twin to turn
items.explanation: When the first twin is cephalic, vaginal birth is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, because the second twin can be delivered by external version or breech extraction by an experienced operator, with cesarean birth held ready. The route depends mainly on the first twin, uncomplicated dichorionic twins are delivered at 38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks, and waiting until 41 weeks raises the risk of stillbirth.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl is 142 cm tall with a webbed neck, no breast development, and primary amenorrhea. Follicle-stimulating hormone is 90 mIU/mL, and the karyotype is 45,X. Which evaluation is needed at diagnosis?
options: Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging
Serum testosterone measurement
Bone age radiograph alone
Echocardiography and renal ultrasonography
items.explanation: Turner syndrome is associated with congenital heart disease, such as bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation, and renal anomalies such as horseshoe kidney, so cardiac imaging and renal ultrasonography are done at diagnosis, along with thyroid and celiac screening. Pituitary imaging is for hypogonadotropic states, and testosterone or bone age alone does not address these risks.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 at 41 0/7 weeks has an uncomplicated pregnancy with a reactive nonstress test, normal amniotic fluid volume, and a closed cervix. She asks about her options. Which counseling is most appropriate?
options: Offer induction now and recommend delivery by 42 0/7 weeks
Expectant management with no testing until 43 weeks
Cesarean birth because the pregnancy is postterm
Weekly membrane sweeping as the only plan
items.explanation: Induction between 41 0/7 and 42 0/7 weeks lowers perinatal mortality and cesarean birth compared with expectant management, so it is offered at 41 weeks and recommended by 42 0/7 weeks, with antenatal testing if the woman chooses to wait. Cesarean birth is not indicated by gestational age alone, waiting until 43 weeks raises stillbirth risk, and membrane sweeping is an adjunct to labor, not a complete plan.

items.stem: A couple has been unable to conceive for 14 months. The man's semen analysis shows azoospermia, volume 0.6 mL, acidic pH, and no fructose. Physical examination shows normal testes but nonpalpable vasa deferentia. Which test is most appropriate next?
options: Varicocelectomy followed by repeat semen analysis
Clomiphene citrate trial for 3 months
Intrauterine insemination with washed sperm
CFTR gene analysis for the patient and his partner
items.explanation: Low volume, acidic pH, absent fructose, and nonpalpable vasa indicate congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, frequently from CFTR mutations, with ejaculatory duct obstruction giving the same chemistry. Testing both partners guides counseling because sperm retrieval and IVF with ICSI risk cystic fibrosis in offspring. Varicocele repair, clomiphene, and insemination cannot help when no sperm are delivered.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 at 9 weeks has persistent vomiting, a 6 kg weight loss, and ketonuria despite pyridoxine and doxylamine. She is admitted for intravenous fluids. Which additional agent should be given before any dextrose-containing solution?
options: Intravenous folic acid
Intravenous vitamin K
Intravenous thiamine
Intramuscular vitamin B12
items.explanation: Prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine, and a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine is given before dextrose-containing fluids while volume and electrolytes are corrected. Folic acid, vitamin K, and vitamin B12 do not prevent this complication, although folate remains part of routine prenatal supplementation. The goal is to avoid encephalopathy with confusion, ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities that can follow refeeding without thiamine.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman requests bilateral tubal sterilization after her second delivery and asks about the risk of failure. Which factor most increases the risk of pregnancy after the procedure over the following decade?
options: Use of partial salpingectomy
Age younger than 30 at the procedure
Breastfeeding at the time of the procedure
A history of two prior vaginal deliveries
items.explanation: In long-term follow-up studies, younger age at sterilization is the strongest predictor of failure, because younger women are more fertile and have more years at risk, and cumulative failure exceeds 1 percent at 10 years. Partial salpingectomy is among the most effective techniques, and breastfeeding and prior vaginal deliveries do not raise failure. Counseling should include this risk and the lower failure rates of long-acting reversible methods.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G1P1 on postoperative day 2 after a cesarean birth that followed prolonged labor has a temperature of 38.7 C, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. The wound is clean and the breasts are soft. Which treatment is recommended?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Intravenous vancomycin alone
Observation with acetaminophen for 24 hours
Intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin
items.explanation: Fever with uterine tenderness and malodorous lochia after cesarean birth is postpartum endometritis, a polymicrobial pelvic infection. Intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin covers anaerobes, gram-negative rods, and many streptococci, and it is continued until the patient has been afebrile for 24 to 48 hours. Oral amoxicillin is inadequate for this severity, vancomycin alone misses gram-negative organisms, and observation delays treatment of a progressive infection.

items.stem: A 43-year-old G3P3 has 2 years of progressively heavier, painful menses. The uterus is uniformly enlarged, globular, and tender, about 12 weeks in size. Endometrial biopsy is benign, and ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous myometrium with small myometrial cysts and no discrete fibroids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Adenomyosis
Submucosal leiomyoma
Endometrial polyp
Endometrial hyperplasia
items.explanation: A uniformly enlarged, globular, tender uterus with heavy painful menses in a multiparous woman in her 40s, with heterogeneous myometrium and myometrial cysts on ultrasonography, indicates adenomyosis. Submucosal fibroids and polyps appear as discrete cavity lesions, and hyperplasia was excluded by the benign biopsy. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy, and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device or hormonal suppression are the medical options.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman reports a certain last menstrual period consistent with 10 weeks 0 days. A first-trimester ultrasonogram measures crown-rump length consistent with 11 weeks 1 day. How should the pregnancy be dated?
options: Keep the menstrual dating, because the last period is certain
Redate by ultrasonography, since the gap exceeds 7 days
Average the two estimates to assign 10 weeks 4 days
Repeat the measurement in 2 weeks before assigning a date
items.explanation: Between 9 0/7 and 13 6/7 weeks, a difference of more than 7 days between menstrual dating and crown-rump length requires redating to the ultrasonographic estimate. A certain last period does not override a discrepancy past the threshold. Averaging has no basis in dating rules, and waiting delays assignment of a gestational age that guides screening and delivery timing.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing endometriosis has a 10 cm unilocular ovarian cyst with a solid mural nodule. Histology shows clear cells and hobnail cells. Which tumor is most likely?
options: Mucinous borderline tumor
Serous cystadenofibroma
Clear cell carcinoma
Mature cystic teratoma
items.explanation: Clear cell carcinoma of the ovary arises in endometriosis and typically presents as a large cyst with a solid mural nodule, with clear and hobnail cells on histology, and it carries a thromboembolic risk and relative chemoresistance. A mucinous borderline tumor has intestinal-type epithelium, a serous cystadenofibroma is benign, and a teratoma contains mature tissues from several germ layers.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman breastfeeding her 6-week-old infant scores 17 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. She has persistent low mood and poor sleep even when the infant sleeps, with no psychotic symptoms, suicidal thoughts, or history of mania. Which medication is a reasonable first-line choice?
options: Lithium carbonate
Sertraline
Daily diazepam
Quetiapine alone
items.explanation: Moderate to severe postpartum depression without psychosis or bipolar features is treated with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor plus psychotherapy, and sertraline is often favored in breastfeeding women because infant exposure through milk is low. Lithium is for bipolar illness and requires infant monitoring, benzodiazepines do not treat depression and cause sedation, and an antipsychotic alone is reserved for psychosis. Breastfeeding need not stop.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with 2 years of infertility is preparing for her first in vitro fertilization cycle. Hysterosalpingography shows bilateral dilated, blocked fallopian tubes, and ultrasonography confirms fluid-filled tubes. What should be done before embryo transfer?
options: Proceed directly to transfer, since tubal disease does not affect IVF
Intrauterine insemination for three cycles
Clomiphene citrate for 6 months
Bilateral salpingectomy or tubal occlusion
items.explanation: A hydrosalpinx lowers the success of in vitro fertilization, probably because tubal fluid drains into the cavity and impairs implantation, and salpingectomy or tubal occlusion before transfer improves the live birth rate and is recommended for most women who have one. Proceeding directly forgoes that gain, insemination fails when the tubes are blocked, and ovulation induction does not bypass tubal obstruction.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 17 weeks has a quadruple screen. Which pattern is most consistent with an increased risk of trisomy 21?
options: High AFP with normal estriol, hCG, and inhibin A
Low AFP, low estriol, low hCG, and low inhibin A
Low AFP and estriol with high hCG and inhibin A
Normal AFP with high estriol and low hCG
items.explanation: Trisomy 21 produces a characteristic quadruple screen pattern of low maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and unconjugated estriol with high hCG and inhibin A. A high AFP suggests an open neural tube defect or abdominal wall defect, a pattern in which all four analytes are low suggests trisomy 18, and normal AFP with high estriol and low hCG matches no common aneuploidy pattern.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 8 months of burning pain at the vaginal entrance with tampon insertion and intercourse. The skin looks normal, and a cotton-swab touch at the vestibule at 5 and 7 o'clock reproduces the pain. Wet mount and cultures are negative. What is the best initial management?
options: Pelvic floor physical therapy with topical lidocaine
Surgical vestibulectomy as the first treatment
Empiric oral fluconazole for 6 months
Topical high-potency corticosteroid ointment
items.explanation: Provoked, localized vestibular pain reproduced by cotton-swab testing, with a normal examination and negative infection testing, defines localized provoked vulvodynia. First-line care is conservative: gentle vulvar hygiene, topical lidocaine, and pelvic floor physical therapy, with neuromodulators or sex therapy added as needed. Vestibulectomy is reserved for refractory disease, antifungals treat an infection that was excluded, and ultrapotent steroids treat lichen sclerosus.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks has sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, and her right calf is swollen and tender. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Which test should be performed first?
options: Quantitative D-dimer to exclude thrombosis
Compression ultrasonography of the right leg
Ventilation-perfusion scan before any other study
Pulmonary angiography with catheter contrast injection
items.explanation: When leg symptoms accompany suspected pulmonary embolism, compression duplex ultrasonography is a radiation-free first step, and a proximal thrombus justifies treatment without chest imaging. D-dimer rises normally in pregnancy and is unreliable, a scan is reserved for those without leg findings and a normal chest radiograph, and catheter angiography is invasive, slower to arrange, and rarely needed in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had no menses for 5 months after a dilation and curettage for retained placenta following delivery. Pregnancy test is negative, and follicle-stimulating hormone and thyroid levels are normal. She has no withdrawal bleeding after estrogen followed by progestin. What is the next step?
options: Pituitary MRI to exclude a mass lesion
Peripheral karyotype for premature ovarian insufficiency
Repeat the progestin challenge with a higher dose
Hysteroscopy to look for intrauterine adhesions
items.explanation: Amenorrhea after uterine curettage with normal gonadotropins and no response to estrogen and progestin points to outflow obstruction from intrauterine adhesions, known as Asherman syndrome. Hysteroscopy confirms the diagnosis and treats it by lysis of adhesions under direct view. A pituitary lesion or ovarian failure would raise or lower gonadotropins, and a larger progestin dose cannot overcome scarred endometrium that is unable to respond.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 36 weeks 0 days has new blood pressures of 144/92 and 148/94 mm Hg four hours apart. Urine protein is negative, platelets and liver enzymes are normal, and she has no symptoms. At what gestational age should delivery be recommended?
options: 37 0/7 weeks
34 0/7 weeks
39 0/7 weeks
40 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: Gestational hypertension without severe features is managed with weekly or more frequent surveillance and delivery at 37 0/7 weeks. Earlier delivery is reserved for severe features, abnormal tests, or fetal compromise, and 34 weeks applies to severe disease that is unstable. Waiting for 39 weeks or beyond 40 weeks raises the risk of progression to preeclampsia and placental complications without benefit.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had four episodes of bacterial vaginosis in 8 months, each resolved by a 7-day course of treatment. Which strategy best reduces recurrence?
options: Routine oral metronidazole treatment of her male partner
Daily vaginal douching with a vinegar solution
Suppressive metronidazole vaginal gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months
Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
items.explanation: For recurrent bacterial vaginosis, extended suppressive therapy with metronidazole vaginal gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months lowers relapse, although recurrence can follow once it stops. Treating male partners has not been shown to reduce recurrence. Douching disturbs the lactobacilli and promotes relapse, and fluconazole treats yeast, which is not the cause here. Patients should understand that relapse remains common even with the best regimen.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 has pushed for 2 hours. The cervix is fully dilated, membranes are ruptured, and the vertex is at plus 2 station in the occiput anterior position. Which additional finding would contraindicate vacuum-assisted delivery?
options: Gestational age of 32 weeks
An estimated fetal weight of 3,600 g
Epidural analgesia in place
Maternal exhaustion with a category I tracing
items.explanation: Vacuum extraction is avoided before 34 weeks because the preterm skull and fragile vessels raise the risk of intracranial and subgaleal hemorrhage. It also requires full dilation, ruptured membranes, an engaged vertex with known position, and an empty bladder. Epidural analgesia, maternal exhaustion, and a normal-sized fetus are accepted settings or indications, and none of them contraindicates the procedure.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian cancer and a pathogenic BRCA1 variant completes optimal cytoreductive surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy with a complete clinical response. Which treatment should be offered next to prolong remission?
options: Tamoxifen for 5 years
Observation only with annual imaging
Hormone therapy with estrogen
Maintenance PARP inhibitor therapy
items.explanation: A BRCA-mutated tumor has defective homologous recombination, so it is highly sensitive to PARP inhibition through synthetic lethality, and maintenance PARP inhibitor therapy after a response to platinum prolongs progression-free survival. Tamoxifen has no role in high-grade serous disease, observation alone forgoes a proven benefit that delays recurrence, and estrogen is not an oncologic therapy and may be harmful.

items.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida has a spontaneous vaginal birth. Examination shows a laceration through the perineal body muscles and the full thickness of both the external and internal anal sphincters, with intact rectal mucosa. How is this injury classified?
options: Second-degree
Third-degree, grade 3c
Fourth-degree
Third-degree, grade 3a
items.explanation: A third-degree laceration involves the anal sphincter complex with intact anorectal mucosa. Grade 3a is less than half the thickness of the external sphincter, 3b is more than half, and 3c involves both external and internal sphincters. A fourth-degree injury also tears the rectal mucosa, and a second-degree injury spares the sphincter entirely, so neither fits the findings described.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman reports urgency, daytime frequency, and leakage before reaching the toilet. Urinalysis is negative, the cough stress test is negative, and postvoid residual is 30 mL. What is the best initial management?
options: Midurethral sling placement under local anesthesia
Cystoscopy with onabotulinumtoxinA injection into the detrusor
Bladder training with pelvic floor muscle exercises
Urodynamic testing before any treatment is started
items.explanation: Urgency incontinence with a negative infection screen and low residual is overactive bladder, and behavioral therapy with timed voiding, bladder training, fluid and caffeine adjustment, and pelvic floor exercises is first line. A sling treats stress incontinence, which she does not have. Botulinum toxin is third-line after drugs fail, and urodynamics are unnecessary before conservative care in uncomplicated cases without complicating features.

items.stem: A 27-year-old multiparous woman in active labor at 5 cm has recurrent late decelerations with moderate variability. Epidural analgesia was placed 20 minutes ago, and her blood pressure is now 84/46 mm Hg. Contractions occur every 3 minutes on oxytocin. What is the best first response?
options: Proceed with immediate cesarean for a category III tracing
Reposition her laterally, give a fluid bolus, and treat the hypotension
Increase the oxytocin rate to improve uterine perfusion
Begin amnioinfusion with warmed saline through the catheter
items.explanation: Recurrent late decelerations with moderate variability form a category II tracing, and maternal hypotension after neuraxial block reduces uteroplacental flow. Lateral positioning, intravenous fluid, and a vasopressor such as ephedrine or phenylephrine correct the cause, and oxytocin is reduced if tachysystole exists. Moderate variability excludes category III, more oxytocin worsens perfusion, and amnioinfusion treats variable decelerations.

items.stem: A 3-year-old girl has labial fusion covering most of the vaginal introitus, with urinary dribbling after voiding and mild vulvar irritation. The examination is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Topical estrogen cream applied to the adhesion
Surgical separation under general anesthesia
Manual separation in the office without anesthesia
A 10-day course of oral antibiotics
items.explanation: Labial adhesions are common in prepubertal girls because low estrogen leaves the labial skin thin, and symptomatic or extensive adhesions are treated with topical estrogen cream, usually with emollients, which separates them over weeks. Surgical or forced manual separation is painful, traumatic, and prone to recurrence, and antibiotics do not treat an adhesion. Barrier ointment after separation lowers the chance of recurrence.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman at 24 weeks is hospitalized with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness, and she improves on intravenous ceftriaxone. She is afebrile for 48 hours and ready for discharge. What is the best measure to prevent recurrence?
options: Repeat urine culture only when symptoms recur, with no antibiotic after discharge
Continue intravenous antibiotics at home for a further 2 weeks
Daily suppressive antibiotic until delivery
Renal ultrasonography with prophylactic ureteral stent placement
items.explanation: Pyelonephritis recurs in a substantial fraction of pregnant women who are not given suppression, so after treatment a daily low-dose antibiotic such as nitrofurantoin is continued through pregnancy, with periodic urine cultures to confirm sterility. Waiting for symptoms to return risks sepsis, extra intravenous therapy adds cost without lowering recurrence, and ureteral stenting is unnecessary when imaging shows no obstruction.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy for fibroids 3 years ago. Her cervix was removed, and pathology showed no cervical neoplasia. She has no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse. What is the recommended cervical cancer screening?
options: Cytology every 3 years until age 65
Cotesting every 5 years until age 65
Annual vaginal vault cytology for life
None; screening is no longer indicated
items.explanation: Women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix for benign reasons and have no history of CIN 2 or worse do not need further screening, because the organ at risk is absent. Cytology of the vaginal vault has a low yield and many false positives. Intervals of 3 or 5 years are meant for women who still have a cervix, and continuing would cause harm without benefit.

items.stem: A 26-year-old at 30 weeks has preterm contractions with cervical dilation of 3 cm. A tocolytic is chosen for 48 hours to allow corticosteroid administration. Which drug carries a risk of premature constriction of the fetal ductus arteriosus?
options: Indomethacin
Nifedipine
Magnesium sulfate
Terbutaline
items.explanation: Indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor, can constrict the fetal ductus arteriosus and also reduces amniotic fluid, so it is limited to gestations under 32 weeks and a short course. Nifedipine causes maternal hypotension and headache, magnesium sulfate causes flushing and respiratory depression in toxicity, and terbutaline causes maternal tachycardia and hyperglycemia. None of those three constricts the ductus.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with 14 months of infertility and regular 28-day cycles is scheduled for hysterosalpingography. When in the cycle should the study be performed?
options: During active menstrual flow, on day 2
At midcycle around ovulation, on day 14
Days 6 to 12, after bleeding stops
In the luteal phase after ovulation, on day 21
items.explanation: Hysterosalpingography is scheduled in the follicular phase after bleeding stops and before ovulation, usually days 6 to 12, so that the endometrium is thin, menstrual debris does not mimic filling defects, and an early pregnancy is excluded. Performing it during bleeding obscures the cavity, at midcycle it risks irradiating a conceptus, and in the luteal phase it may disturb a possible implantation.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 28 weeks has a velamentous cord insertion, and color Doppler ultrasonography shows fetal vessels crossing over the internal os. She has no bleeding or contractions. What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Induction of labor at 39 weeks with continuous monitoring
Scheduled cesarean at 39 0/7 weeks to allow lung maturity
Expectant management until labor, then cesarean once contractions begin
Scheduled cesarean between 34 0/7 and 37 0/7 weeks
items.explanation: Vasa previa risks fetal exsanguination when membranes rupture or the cervix dilates, since unprotected vessels tear. Prenatally diagnosed cases do best with scheduled cesarean at 34 0/7 to 37 0/7 weeks, sometimes with antenatal admission. Waiting for labor or for a term date exposes the fetus to rupture, and vaginal birth is contraindicated with vessels over the os.

items.stem: Three weeks after a hysterectomy for fibroids, a 46-year-old woman reports continuous watery vaginal discharge. Dilute methylene blue is instilled into the bladder, and a vaginal tampon remains white but is wet with clear fluid after 30 minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vesicovaginal fistula
Ureterovaginal fistula
Urethral diverticulum
Stress urinary incontinence
items.explanation: When dye placed in the bladder does not stain the tampon but clear fluid still leaks, the leak is not from the bladder, so a ureterovaginal fistula is suspected and confirmed with CT urography or retrograde pyelography. Staining of the tampon would indicate a vesicovaginal fistula. A diverticulum causes postvoid dribbling and dyspareunia, and stress incontinence leaks only with exertion.

items.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks is 6 cm dilated, and oligohydramnios was noted earlier. Recurrent variable decelerations with slow return to baseline and moderate variability persist after repositioning and stopping oxytocin. What is the next intervention?
options: Terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously
Immediate cesarean for a category III tracing
Amnioinfusion
Magnesium sulfate loading dose
items.explanation: Variable decelerations arise from cord compression, which is more likely with low fluid volume. Amnioinfusion with isotonic fluid restores a cushion and reduces the frequency and depth of decelerations. Terbutaline is used for tachysystole, moderate variability keeps this tracing in category II so immediate surgery is not mandatory, and magnesium has no effect on cord compression.

items.stem: A 28-year-old at 33 weeks has regular contractions and the cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80% effaced. She has received no corticosteroids this pregnancy. Which regimen is recommended?
options: Betamethasone 12 mg intramuscularly every week until delivery
Betamethasone 12 mg intramuscularly, two doses 24 hours apart
Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously every 8 hours for 3 doses
Prednisone 40 mg orally daily for 5 days
items.explanation: A single course of betamethasone, two intramuscular doses 24 hours apart, between 24 and 34 weeks reduces respiratory distress, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neonatal death when birth is expected within 7 days. Weekly courses add no benefit and may impair growth. Hydrocortisone and prednisone are largely inactivated by placental enzymes, so little active drug reaches the fetus.

items.stem: A 36-year-old G5P4 has uterine atony after delivery of a 4,300 g infant. She has chronic hypertension and asthma, and bleeding continues after oxytocin infusion and fundal massage. Which agent is the most appropriate next choice?
options: Misoprostol 800 mcg rectally
Methylergonovine 0.2 mg intramuscularly
Carboprost tromethamine 250 mcg intramuscularly
Oxytocin 40 units as an undiluted intravenous push
items.explanation: Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analogue, has no effect on blood pressure or bronchial tone, so it suits a woman who has both of these conditions. Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertension. Carboprost can provoke bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma. A rapid undiluted oxytocin bolus causes profound hypotension and arrhythmia, so it is always given as a dilute infusion.
