items.stem: A 27-year-old woman had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect and now plans a new pregnancy. She takes no medications. Which folic acid recommendation is correct?
options: 0.4 mg daily starting at the first prenatal visit
1 mg daily starting in the second trimester
4 mg daily after the anatomy scan shows normal spine
4 mg daily beginning at least 1 month before conception
items.explanation: A prior pregnancy with a neural tube defect carries a recurrence risk near 3 percent, and high-dose folic acid of 4 mg daily, started at least a month before conception and continued through the first trimester, reduces recurrence by most of that risk. Standard doses of 0.4 mg are for average-risk women. Starting after conception or after an ultrasound is too late for neural tube closure, which finishes by about 6 weeks.

items.stem: A 30-year-old primipara delivers a healthy infant after an uncomplicated labor. Oxytocin was given with the anterior shoulder. Thirty minutes later the placenta has not delivered, there is minimal bleeding, and she is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait for a further hour before intervening
Dilation and curettage in the operating room immediately
Manual removal of the placenta under adequate analgesia
Intramuscular methylergonovine, then observe for 60 minutes
items.explanation: A retained placenta is diagnosed when delivery has not occurred by about 30 minutes, and manual removal with analgesia is the standard when attempts at controlled traction fail, since delay raises hemorrhage and infection risk. Waiting longer without a reason adds risk, curettage is for remnants after the placenta is out, and an ergot agent can trap the placenta by causing a constriction ring.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman 4 weeks postpartum was treated for mastitis for 3 days but still has fever and now has a tender 4 cm fluctuant area in the breast. What is the best next step?
options: Ultrasonography with needle aspiration or drainage of the collection
Switch to oral antibiotics and wait another week
Stop breastfeeding abruptly with a tight binder
Screening mammography
items.explanation: Failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics with a fluctuant mass suggests a breast abscess, which is confirmed by ultrasonography and treated with aspiration or drainage plus antibiotics, while nursing continues. Waiting longer delays drainage and risks spread. Abrupt weaning worsens engorgement, and mammography is not the tool for puerperal infection. Continued milk removal helps resolution of the infection.

items.stem: At 35 weeks, a 35-year-old patient has a complete placenta previa without evidence of accreta. She has had no bleeding since a single episode at 28 weeks. When should delivery be planned?
options: Cesarean at 34 0/7 weeks regardless of fetal maturity
Induction of labor at 39 0/7 weeks with close monitoring
Cesarean at 39 0/7 weeks after confirmation of lung maturity
Cesarean at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: Placenta previa without accreta is delivered by scheduled cesarean at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks, balancing the risk of antepartum hemorrhage against neonatal immaturity. Earlier birth is reserved for repeated bleeding or instability. Labor is contraindicated with previa over the os, and waiting until 39 weeks increases the chance of emergency delivery during a sudden bleed.

items.stem: Because of advanced maternal age, a 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks undergoes chorionic villus sampling. The villi show mosaicism for trisomy 16, and an ultrasonogram shows a structurally normal fetus. What is the best next step?
options: Accept the villi result as the fetal karyotype and counsel accordingly
Amniocentesis to determine whether the fetus itself is mosaic
Repeat chorionic villus sampling at a different placental site
Cell-free DNA screening to settle the question definitively
items.explanation: Villi originate from trophoblast, and an abnormal mosaic line may be confined to the placenta without affecting the fetus. Amniocentesis samples fetal cells and clarifies whether true fetal mosaicism exists. Treating the result as the fetal karyotype risks needless alarm, repeat sampling gives the same placental tissue, and cell-free DNA is also placental in origin and cannot resolve the problem.
